set.stem: A 72-year-old woman with ischaemic cardiomyopathy and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% has NYHA class II symptoms. She takes lisinopril 40 mg daily, carvedilol 25 mg twice daily and spironolactone 25 mg daily. Blood pressure is 102/82 mmHg and she is in sinus rhythm at 60 beats/min. Her eGFR is 55 mL/min/1.73 m² and potassium 4.8 mmol/L. Which additional medication will further reduce her mortality?
topics: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
set.explanation: The four pillars of HFrEF therapy are an ACE inhibitor (or sacubitril/valsartan), a beta-blocker, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and an SGLT2 inhibitor; dapagliflozin (DAPA-HF) and empagliflozin (EMPEROR-Reduced) reduce cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalisation whether or not the patient has diabetes, and should be added here. Adding valsartan or aliskiren to an ACE inhibitor plus MRA increases hyperkalaemia and renal failure without survival benefit, digoxin reduces admissions but not mortality, and ivabradine is only for sinus rhythm of 70 beats/min or more despite maximal beta-blockade. Replacing lisinopril with sacubitril/valsartan is a further option if she stays symptomatic.

why: Original key 'none of the above' is outdated; SGLT2 inhibitors now reduce mortality on top of ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker and MRA (option E replaced with dapagliflozin; distinct from hf-0071)

set.stem: A 57-year-old man had a large anterior myocardial infarction 8 months ago, treated with primary PCI with an excellent result despite a late presentation. He is now asymptomatic on optimal medical therapy, with heart rate 65 beats/min and blood pressure 104/82 mmHg. His ECG shows sinus rhythm with right bundle branch block and a QRS duration of 135 ms. Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 25% with a large anterior dyskinetic area consistent with aneurysm. Which therapy is indicated to reduce his mortality?
set.explanation: More than 40 days after MI (and at least 3 months after revascularisation), an ischaemic cardiomyopathy with EF of 30% or less carries a high risk of sudden arrhythmic death, and a primary-prevention ICD reduces mortality even in mildly symptomatic or asymptomatic patients (MADIT-II). Cardiac resynchronisation is indicated mainly for left bundle branch block with QRS of 150 ms or more (at least 130 ms), not RBBB of 135 ms. Ivabradine needs a sinus rate of 70/min or more and does not reduce mortality in this setting, and surgical ventricular restoration did not improve survival in the STICH trial.

set.stem: A 25-year-old man had an orthotopic heart transplant for non-ischaemic cardiomyopathy 18 months ago. His resting heart rate has been consistently around 90 beats/min, and he feels well. What is the most appropriate next step regarding his resting heart rate?
set.explanation: The transplanted heart is denervated, so without vagal tone its SA node runs at the intrinsic rate of about 90–110 beats/min, and a steady resting rate of 90 in a well patient is expected. Reassurance is appropriate. Rate-slowing drugs are unnecessary and blunt the catecholamine-dependent response to exercise, and there is no reason to suspect ectopic atrial tachycardia or to test chronotropic competence in an asymptomatic patient.

set.stem: A government committee on organ transplantation is considering a nationwide sharing strategy for donor hearts in a large country. Why is such a strategy not beneficial?
options: Blood groups are distributed non-randomly across the country, preventing true nationwide sharing
Regions use highly variable criteria for grading severity of illness
The financial structure of reimbursement would not allow it
The tolerable cold ischaemic time of a harvested heart is too short to allow nationwide sharing
set.explanation: A donor heart tolerates only about 4 hours of cold ischaemic time before graft function deteriorates, so hearts must be allocated within a limited geographical radius of the donor, with priority given to the sickest recipients (and waiting time and blood group compatibility also counted). Longer distances raise the risk of primary graft failure, although newer normothermic ex vivo perfusion systems are beginning to extend this window. Blood-group distribution, regional criteria and finance are not the fundamental limits.

set.stem: A 68-year-old woman with chemotherapy-related cardiomyopathy (EF 15%) has frequent admissions with acute decompensated heart failure despite optimal therapy. She is not a candidate for heart transplantation. Which of the following statements about other options to prolong her life is correct?
set.explanation: In advanced (stage D) heart failure in patients ineligible for transplant, a durable left ventricular assist device as destination therapy improves survival and quality of life compared with medical therapy (REMATCH, with better results from modern continuous-flow devices such as HeartMate 3). Continuous inotropes such as milrinone relieve symptoms or bridge to a decision but do not improve, and may worsen, survival, and stem-cell therapy has no proven mortality benefit. Palliative care should be integrated alongside, but it is not true that no life-prolonging options exist.

set.stem: Which of the following statements regarding the epidemiology of congenital heart disease (CHD) in high-income countries is true?
options: CHD is extremely rare, complicating fewer than 1 in 1000 live births
With advances in surgery and pre- and postnatal care, survival of neonates with CHD now approaches 90%
Because fewer women with CHD become pregnant, the incidence of CHD in neonates is declining
The population of adults with CHD is declining because of improved prenatal screening
Women with CHD have no increased risk of complications during pregnancy compared with the general population
set.explanation: CHD affects about 1% (roughly 8 per 1000) of live births, and with modern surgical, catheter and perinatal care about 90% of affected neonates now survive to adulthood. As a result, adults with CHD now outnumber children with CHD and the adult population is growing, not shrinking. More women with CHD reach childbearing age and become pregnant, and they face higher risks of heart failure, arrhythmia and obstetric complications and a higher (about 3–5%) risk of CHD in their offspring.

set.stem: A 62-year-old man is being assessed for mitral valve surgery for severe mitral regurgitation. Transoesophageal echocardiography shows a small jet of right-to-left flow across the atrial septum, occurring when a small flap of tissue swings open (less than 1 mm). Which of the following explains this finding?
set.explanation: A patent foramen ovale is present in about 25% of adults: the septum primum flap fails to fuse with the septum secundum, forming a valve-like channel that opens intermittently when right atrial pressure exceeds left (e.g. with coughing or Valsalva), allowing small right-to-left shunts and paradoxical embolism. Secundum, primum and sinus venosus ASDs are true tissue deficiencies with a persistent, usually left-to-right, shunt, and partial anomalous pulmonary venous return drains pulmonary veins into the right side. An incidental PFO needs no treatment; closure is considered after cryptogenic stroke in younger patients.

set.stem: A 21-year-old man has a newly diagnosed ventricular septal defect (VSD). Echocardiography confirms a 5-mm VSD in the muscular interventricular septum. Right heart catheterisation shows a mean pulmonary artery pressure of 20 mmHg, pulmonary vascular resistance of 2 Wood units and systemic vascular resistance of 6 Wood units, with a Qp:Qs of 1.25. What do you recommend?
set.explanation: This is a small restrictive muscular VSD with a Qp:Qs below 1.5, normal pulmonary pressure and resistance and, presumably, no LV volume overload, so closure is not indicated and he needs periodic review. Closure (surgical patch or percutaneous device) is considered when Qp:Qs is 1.5 or more with LV volume overload, after endocarditis, or with aortic cusp prolapse; transplantation is only for established Eisenmenger physiology. Good dental hygiene is advised because of the lifelong endocarditis risk.

set.stem: A 52-year-old patient presents with chest pain and raised cardiac enzymes. A superficial continuous murmur, not previously documented, is heard at the mid-sternal level. Echocardiography shows normal valves. Right heart catheterisation gives these oxygen saturations: superior vena cava 58%, right atrium 60%, mid-coronary sinus 91%, right ventricle 70%, pulmonary artery 70%. What abnormality accounts for these findings?
set.explanation: A saturation of 91% in the coronary sinus, which normally carries the most desaturated blood in the body (about 30–40%), means arterial blood is entering it directly: a coronary artery fistula draining into the coronary sinus. The fistula produces a continuous murmur and can cause myocardial ischaemia through coronary steal, explaining the chest pain and enzyme rise. ASD would cause a step-up in the right atrium, VSD in the right ventricle and PDA in the pulmonary artery, while an anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery presents mainly in infancy. Treatment is closure by catheter or surgery.

set.stem: A 40-year-old man has a congenital bicuspid aortic valve. Which other structure is important to follow on his regular echocardiograms?
set.explanation: Bicuspid aortic valve is associated with an intrinsic aortopathy (medial degeneration), so the aortic root and ascending aorta dilate independently of valve function, risking aneurysm and dissection. Imaging should measure the valve and the aorta, with CT or MRI if the ascending aorta is not well seen; surgery is considered at a diameter of 55 mm, or 50 mm with risk factors. Coarctation should also be excluded, as it frequently coexists.

set.stem: All of the following are classic defining features of tetralogy of Fallot EXCEPT:
set.explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot results from anterior deviation of the outlet septum and comprises a large ventricular septal defect, an overriding aorta, right ventricular outflow tract (usually infundibular) obstruction and right ventricular hypertrophy. Tricuspid atresia is a separate cyanotic lesion with an absent tricuspid valve and a hypoplastic right ventricle. Tetralogy is the commonest cyanotic congenital lesion beyond infancy and is repaired surgically in the first year of life.

At 78, severe aortic stenosis is most often degenerative calcific disease of a trileaflet valve, an active process resembling atherosclerosis whose risk factors include age, diabetes, hypertension, smoking, dyslipidaemia (including raised lipoprotein(a)) and chronic kidney disease. A bicuspid valve usually presents with stenosis earlier (typically at 50–70 years), rheumatic aortic stenosis almost always coexists with mitral disease, and connective tissue disorders cause regurgitation rather than stenosis.

set.stem: A 63-year-old man presents with new exertional syncope and is found to have severe aortic stenosis. What is the average life expectancy of untreated patients with this presentation?
set.explanation: Severe aortic stenosis has a long latent period, but once symptoms appear prognosis without valve replacement is poor: average survival is about 5 years after angina, 3 years after syncope and 2 years after heart failure (and less than 1 year with atrial fibrillation). Any symptom attributable to severe aortic stenosis is therefore an indication for surgical or transcatheter aortic valve replacement.

In cardiogenic shock from critical aortic stenosis, percutaneous balloon aortic valvuloplasty can relieve the obstruction temporarily and stabilise the patient as a bridge to definitive surgical or transcatheter valve replacement. Its benefit is short-lived because restenosis is common within months. Beta-blockers reduce contractility and can precipitate collapse, digoxin and statins have no acute role, and phenylephrine raises afterload against a fixed obstruction; intravenous nitroprusside can be used cautiously under invasive monitoring in decompensated patients without hypotension.

set.stem: An 85-year-old man presents with increasing breathlessness and leg oedema. Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 25% with global hypokinesis, a calculated aortic valve area of 0.8 cm² and a mean gradient of 25 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step to determine whether he would benefit from aortic valve replacement?
set.explanation: A small calculated valve area with a low gradient and poor EF is low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis: either true severe stenosis causing LV failure or a moderately stenosed valve that the weak ventricle cannot open fully (pseudo-severe stenosis). Low-dose dobutamine stress echo distinguishes them: in true stenosis the gradient rises (mean 40 mmHg or more) while the area stays at or below 1.0 cm², and it also shows contractile (flow) reserve, which predicts surgical outcome. CT calcium scoring of the valve is an alternative, whereas MRI, PET, angiography and right heart catheterisation do not answer this question.

In chronic severe aortic regurgitation, blood leaks back into the LV during diastole, so aortic diastolic pressure falls and pulse pressure widens (collapsing pulse and other peripheral signs). The LV adapts with eccentric hypertrophy and dilatation, so LV end-diastolic volume (preload) and total stroke volume increase, and the large stroke volume ejected into the aorta raises systolic pressure and wall stress, increasing afterload.

set.stem: A 21-year-old woman with a connective tissue disease presents with acute breathlessness and pulmonary oedema. Echocardiography shows severe aortic regurgitation with an avulsed right coronary cusp. While awaiting emergency surgery, which intervention is most likely to help maintain her end-organ perfusion?
set.explanation: In acute severe aortic regurgitation the non-dilated LV cannot accommodate the regurgitant volume, so filling pressure rises steeply and forward output falls. Nitroprusside lowers systemic resistance, reducing the regurgitant fraction and increasing forward flow, often with an inotrope such as dobutamine, as a bridge to urgent valve surgery. An intra-aortic balloon pump is contraindicated because diastolic inflation worsens regurgitation, beta-blockers prolong diastole and increase regurgitation, and vasoconstrictors such as noradrenaline or vasopressin raise afterload.

set.stem: What is the most common cause of obstruction to left ventricular inflow worldwide?
set.explanation: Rheumatic heart disease is by far the commonest cause of mitral stenosis and of LV inflow obstruction worldwide, producing commissural fusion, leaflet thickening and chordal shortening years after acute rheumatic fever. In older patients in high-income countries, degenerative mitral annular calcification is an increasing cause, while congenital mitral stenosis, cor triatriatum, left atrial myxoma and large vegetations are rare causes.

In mitral stenosis, a pressure gradient is needed to drive blood across the narrowed valve, so left atrial pressure rises (transmitted back as pulmonary venous congestion and eventually pulmonary hypertension, which lowers pulmonary vascular compliance). The LV itself is underfilled: LV end-diastolic pressure and diameter are normal or low and cardiac output is reduced, especially on exercise.

set.stem: In a patient with mitral stenosis, all of the following will raise left atrial pressure and may worsen pulmonary congestion EXCEPT:
set.explanation: The transmitral gradient depends on flow and on diastolic filling time, so anything that increases cardiac output or heart rate (anaemia, pregnancy, exercise, fever, thyrotoxicosis, AF, or beta-agonists such as isoprenaline) raises left atrial pressure and can precipitate pulmonary oedema. Beta-blockers such as metoprolol slow the heart, prolonging diastole and lowering the gradient and left atrial pressure, so they are used to relieve exertional symptoms and control rate.

set.stem: An 84-year-old woman with severe mitral stenosis develops new-onset atrial fibrillation. Which of the following interventions will NOT help lower her left atrial pressure?
set.explanation: Left atrial pressure in mitral stenosis falls with less volume (diuretics), a larger valve orifice (balloon mitral valvotomy) and a slower rate with atrial contraction restored (cardioversion, beta-blockers or rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers). Pacing at 90 beats/min would shorten diastolic filling time, raising the gradient and left atrial pressure. Patients with mitral stenosis and AF also need anticoagulation with warfarin.

set.stem: A 34-year-old man with rheumatic mitral stenosis is asymptomatic, with a mitral valve area of 1.7 cm². On exercise his pulmonary artery systolic pressure reaches 40 mmHg. What management do you recommend?
set.explanation: A mitral valve area of 1.7 cm² is moderate stenosis (severe is 1.5 cm² or less), he has no symptoms, and the exercise pulmonary artery pressure is below the 60 mmHg threshold that would support intervention, so he needs clinical review and serial echocardiography (about every 1–2 years). Balloon valvotomy or surgery is reserved for severe stenosis with symptoms, or selected asymptomatic patients with severe stenosis and high embolic risk or pulmonary hypertension. Beta-blockers are only for symptom relief, and sildenafil has no role.

set.stem: A 65-year-old man with a 15-year history of non-ischaemic dilated cardiomyopathy (LVEF 30%) has severe functional (secondary) mitral regurgitation. He remains in NYHA class III despite optimal guideline-directed medical therapy and cardiac resynchronisation. He asks whether fixing his valve would improve his survival. What is the most accurate response?
options: Valve repair is only needed if you develop pulmonary hypertension or atrial fibrillation
Neither surgical nor percutaneous valve repair has ever been shown to improve survival in patients like you
Surgery should be considered only if repair is possible, because replacement would not improve survival
Surgical repair has not been shown to improve survival, but in selected patients like you transcatheter edge-to-edge repair has been shown to reduce mortality
Yes, your valve should have been fixed years ago
set.explanation: In secondary mitral regurgitation the leaflets are normal and the leak results from LV dilatation, so the disease is ventricular and surgical repair or replacement has not been shown to prolong life. However, in the COAPT trial, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (MitraClip) reduced heart-failure admissions and all-cause mortality in patients who stayed symptomatic despite optimised medical and device therapy, with a moderately dilated LV (MITRA-FR, with more dilated ventricles, was neutral). ESC and ACC/AHA guidelines therefore support this procedure in carefully selected patients.

why: The COAPT trial showed a mortality benefit from transcatheter edge-to-edge repair in selected secondary MR; the old key (repair never improves survival) is outdated. Stem given the selection details and options rewritten

set.stem: During right and left heart catheterisation of a patient with stenosis of two valves, the following pressures are recorded: right atrium (mean) 15 mmHg; right ventricle 25/6 mmHg; pulmonary artery 25/12 mmHg; pulmonary artery wedge pressure 12 mmHg; left ventricle 105/6 mmHg; aorta 105/75 mmHg. Which two valves are stenosed?
set.explanation: A diastolic gradient across a valve indicates stenosis. The mean right atrial pressure (15 mmHg) exceeds RV end-diastolic pressure (6 mmHg), showing tricuspid stenosis, and the wedge pressure (12 mmHg, reflecting left atrial pressure) exceeds LV end-diastolic pressure (6 mmHg), showing mitral stenosis. There is no systolic gradient between RV and pulmonary artery (both 25 mmHg) or between LV and aorta (both 105 mmHg), so pulmonary and aortic valves are not stenosed. Combined mitral and tricuspid stenosis is typical of rheumatic heart disease.

set.explanation: Her tricuspid regurgitation is functional, caused by RV dilatation and annular stretching secondary to pulmonary hypertension, not by leaflet disease. Treatment targets the cause: diuretics and salt restriction for congestion and pulmonary vasodilator therapy (e.g. endothelin receptor antagonists, PDE-5 inhibitors, prostanoids) to unload the RV. Isolated tricuspid surgery or percutaneous repair carries high risk and little benefit with severe pulmonary hypertension and RV dysfunction, balloon valvotomy treats stenosis, and her mitral valve is normal.

set.stem: A 21-year-old woman who has never seen a doctor is found to have an ejection systolic murmur in the left second intercostal space, preceded by an ejection click. Echocardiography confirms pulmonary stenosis with a peak gradient of 70 mmHg and a doming pulmonary valve without regurgitation. What is the best treatment?
set.explanation: A thin, mobile, doming pulmonary valve (with an ejection click that softens on inspiration) is typical congenital valvular pulmonary stenosis. Intervention is indicated for a peak gradient above about 60–64 mmHg even without symptoms, or with symptoms or RV dysfunction, and percutaneous balloon valvotomy is the treatment of choice, with excellent long-term results. Valve replacement is reserved for dysplastic valves or significant regurgitation, and diuretics do not treat the obstruction.

why: 'Presystolic click' corrected to ejection click; peak gradient raised from 60 to 70 mmHg so it clearly exceeds the ESC intervention threshold (64 mmHg)

set.explanation: New severe mitral regurgitation gives the LV a low-pressure escape route into the left atrium, so total ejection and ejection fraction rise even though forward stroke volume falls. With less forward flow across the aortic valve, the aortic gradient falls (risking underestimation of stenosis severity), and the calculated valve area is not truly changed. LV afterload falls rather than rises because part of the stroke volume is ejected into the low-pressure atrium.

set.stem: A man with rheumatic heart disease and moderate mitral stenosis presents with atrial fibrillation at a ventricular rate of 60 beats/min. Which of the following is the appropriate thromboembolic prophylaxis?
set.explanation: AF with moderate or severe rheumatic mitral stenosis carries a very high thromboembolic risk, so anticoagulation is indicated regardless of the CHA₂DS₂-VASc score. A vitamin K antagonist (warfarin, INR 2–3) is recommended: these patients were excluded from DOAC trials, and in the INVICTUS trial rivaroxaban was inferior to warfarin in rheumatic heart disease with AF. DOACs (apixaban, dabigatran, rivaroxaban) are also contraindicated with mechanical valves, but can be used in AF with most other native valve disease.

why: 'Moderate mitral stenosis' added to the stem: DOACs are acceptable in AF with many other rheumatic lesions, so warfarin is the single best answer only with mitral stenosis

set.explanation: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is LV systolic dysfunction (EF usually below 45%) developing late in pregnancy or in the months after delivery without another cause. Risk factors include older maternal age, multiparity, multiple pregnancy, pre-eclampsia and hypertension, African ancestry, malnutrition and prolonged tocolytic therapy; primiparity is not a classic risk factor. Treatment follows heart-failure principles (ACE inhibitors only after delivery), with bromocriptine considered to block the cleaved prolactin fragment implicated in its pathogenesis.
